title: Why should stream pipelines be side-effect-free — why is mutating an external collection/variable from inside forEach/map/filter a bug (unpredictable with parallel streams, breaks laziness, not thread-safe) — and what is the correct approach (use collect/reduce instead of shared ArrayList)?
shortTitle: Side-effect-free pipelines — why mutating external state from forEach/map/filter is a bug

s1_definition.profdef: Stream pipelines should be SIDE-EFFECT-FREE: intermediate operations (filter, map, flatMap) and ideally forEach should NOT mutate external state (shared variables, external collections, class fields). Why: (1) PARALLEL STREAMS — multiple threads execute the pipeline concurrently; mutating a shared ArrayList causes ConcurrentModificationException or data corruption, (2) LAZINESS — the JVM can reorder, skip, or re-run operations during optimization; side effects may execute in unexpected order or not at all, (3) NOT THREAD-SAFE — ArrayList.add() from multiple threads loses elements, (4) REPRODUCIBILITY — side effects make debugging impossible because behavior depends on timing. The correct approach: use `collect(Collectors.toList())` or `reduce()` to PRODUCE the result, not build it manually inside forEach.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine 10 bank clerks (parallel threads) each adding entries to ONE shared ledger book (shared ArrayList). Clerk A writes line 5, Clerk B writes line 5 at the same time — one entry is LOST. Clerk C writes on page 2 while Clerk D flips to page 3 — entries are SCRAMBLED. The correct approach: each clerk has their OWN notepad (thread-local accumulation), and at the end, a supervisor MERGES all notepads into the final ledger (collect/reduce). This is exactly what Collectors do internally.
s1_definition.oneliner: Never mutate shared state inside map/filter/forEach. Use collect() or reduce() to produce results. Parallel streams + shared mutable state = data corruption. Side-effect-free = safe, reproducible, parallelizable.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Stream pipelines should be SIDE-EFFECT-FREE: intermediate operations (filter, map, flatMap) and ideally forEach should NOT mutate external state (shared variables, external collections, class fields). Why: (1) PARALLEL STREAMS — multiple threads execute the pipeline concurrently; mutating a shared ArrayList causes ConcurrentModificationException or data corruption, (2) LAZINESS — the JVM can reorder, skip, or re-run operations during optimization; side effects may execute in unexpected order or not at all, (3) NOT THREAD-SAFE — ArrayList.add() from multiple threads loses elements, (4) REPRODUCIBILITY — side effects make debugging impossible because behavior depends on timing. The correct approach: use `collect(Collectors.toList())` or `reduce()` to PRODUCE the result, not build it manually inside forEach.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine 10 bank clerks (parallel threads) each adding entries to ONE shared ledger book (shared ArrayList). Clerk A writes line 5, Clerk B writes line 5 at the same time — one entry is LOST. Clerk C writes on page 2 while Clerk D flips to page 3 — entries are SCRAMBLED. The correct approach: each clerk has their OWN notepad (thread-local accumulation), and at the end, a supervisor MERGES all notepads into the final ledger (collect/reduce). This is exactly what Collectors do internally.

**One line to remember:** Never mutate shared state inside map/filter/forEach. Use collect() or reduce() to produce results. Parallel streams + shared mutable state = data corruption. Side-effect-free = safe, reproducible, parallelizable.

sections.s3_banking: **Problem — The bank's parallel batch processor builds a settlement report by adding entries to a shared ArrayList from multiple threads.** Under load, the report has missing entries (lost in race conditions), duplicate entries (parallel forEach with add), and scrambled order. The fix: replace forEach+shared list with collect(Collectors.toList()), collect(groupingBy), and reduce.

sections.s5_journey:
**Step 1 — Unsafe.** 10,000 elements processed by `parallelStream()`. ForkJoinPool spawns 7 threads.

**Step 2.** All 7 threads call `results.add(element)` on the SAME ArrayList simultaneously. ArrayList.add internally: checks capacity → maybe resize array → write at index → increment size. Two threads read size=5000, both write at index 5000, both increment to 5001 → ONE element LOST.

**Step 3.** Result: expected 10,000, got 9,847 — 153 entries vanished. Sometimes: ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException when resize happens during concurrent write.

**Step 4 — Safe (collect).** `collect(Collectors.toList())` internally: creates a NEW ArrayList per thread (supplier), each thread adds to its OWN list (accumulator), then lists are MERGED (combiner: addAll). No shared state during processing. Thread A: [T-1, T-2...], Thread B: [T-3, T-4...]. Merge: [T-1, T-2, T-3, T-4...]. Always 10,000.

**Step 5 — Safe (reduce).** `reduce(0, Integer::sum)` is associative: (a+b)+c = a+(b+c). Each thread reduces its partition: Thread A: 1+2+3...=X, Thread B: 4+5+6...=Y. Final: X+Y+Z = 50,005,000. Always correct.
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ═══ UNSAFE: shared ArrayList + parallel ═══

  ForkJoinPool Thread 1 ──┐
  ForkJoinPool Thread 2 ──┤──→ shared ArrayList.add() ──→ 💥 RACE CONDITION!
  ForkJoinPool Thread 3 ──┤    Thread 1: read size=5000, write index 5000
  ForkJoinPool Thread 4 ──┘    Thread 2: read size=5000, write index 5000 ← OVERWRITE!
                                Result: 9,847 of 10,000 (153 LOST)

  ═══ SAFE: collect(Collectors.toList()) ═══

  Thread 1 → OWN ArrayList [T-1, T-4, T-7...]     ← thread-local, no sharing!
  Thread 2 → OWN ArrayList [T-2, T-5, T-8...]     ← thread-local
  Thread 3 → OWN ArrayList [T-3, T-6, T-9...]     ← thread-local
             │
             └── MERGE (combiner: addAll) ──→ Final List [all 10,000]  ✅

  Collector internals:
    supplier:    () → new ArrayList<>()     (one per thread)
    accumulator: (list, element) → list.add(element)   (thread-local)
    combiner:    (list1, list2) → list1.addAll(list2)  (merge phase)

  ═══ RULE: SIDE-EFFECT-FREE ═══

  ❌ forEach + shared.add()     → use collect(toList())
  ❌ filter + counter++          → use count()
  ❌ map + auditLog.add()        → use peek() for debug only
  ❌ forEach + accumulator       → use reduce(identity, BinaryOp)
  ❌ external HashMap mutation   → use collect(groupingBy())
```

  │  ──────────────────────────────────── │

  │  ✗ UNSAFE: forEach(sharedList::add)   │  loses records in parallel

sections.s6_takeaway:
Stream pipelines should be side-effect-free: intermediate operations like filter, map, and flatMap should not mutate external state — shared variables, collections, or fields. The primary reason is parallel safety: with parallelStream, multiple ForkJoinPool threads execute the pipeline concurrently. Mutating a shared ArrayList from forEach causes race conditions — ArrayList.add is not thread-safe, leading to lost elements, ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, or corrupted internal state. Even with synchronizedList, the order of side effects is unpredictable in parallel.

In my safe pipeline service, the unsafe version adds 10,000 elements to a shared ArrayList from a parallel stream and consistently loses entries — typically 100-200 out of 10,000 are silently dropped due to concurrent writes. The safe version uses collect(Collectors.toList()), which handles parallelism internally: it creates a separate ArrayList per thread (supplier), each thread accumulates into its own list (accumulator), and lists are merged after processing (combiner). Zero shared mutable state during execution means zero data loss — always exactly 10,000 elements.

The rule is simple: use collect() to produce collections, reduce() to produce values, count() to count, and avoid forEach with external mutation. If you must perform side effects (logging, database writes), use forEach at the END of the pipeline and accept that in parallel streams the order is non-deterministic — use forEachOrdered() if order matters, but it defeats parallelism. The broader principle: streams are designed for functional-style programming where data flows through transformations and results are produced, not accumulated into shared state.
